voice.text: Two window shapes. One concentrates more stress. Look at the corners. Which would you trust?
At cruising altitude, the outside air is thin. The cabin holds air at higher pressure.
That difference pushes outward on the fuselage. The aircraft skin carries this load around the windows.
In cross section, air pushes outward in every direction. The shell stretches like a balloon.
The pressure difference rises during a climb and falls on descent. Every flight repeats the load.
Cut a hole in that skin and forces must travel through the metal around the opening.

annotations.text: Load paths bend around an opening

voice.text: A sharp corner forces an abrupt turn. The local stress can spike right at that corner.
A wider curve eases that turn. Stress still concentrates, but rounding reduces the peak.

annotations.text: A gentler turn for the load

voice.text: Repeated loads can grow a small crack, a little at a time. Engineers call this fatigue.
In the nineteen fifties, Comet jet crashes prompted an investigation into fatigue in the pressure cabin.
Investigators pressurized a test fuselage in a water tank and watched cracks grow across repeated cycles.
In one crash, fatigue evidence pointed to a radio antenna opening. Fastener details mattered too.
Engineers also reinforce the frame and test for fatigue. The window shape is part of a system.
Back at your seat, the window might look oval or rectangular. Look for the smoothly rounded corners.
Those curves reduce local stress. That is why the corners are built for flight after flight.
